source.title: Observational properties of diffuse radio sources in Galaxy Clusters: Current knowledge and open questions

accepted.question_text: What physical mechanism produces radio mini-halos in relaxed galaxy clusters, where a central radio active galactic nucleus is surrounded by diffuse steep-spectrum radio emission with spectral index α > 1 and a linear extent of a few hundred kiloparsecs, given that the diffusion time of relativistic electrons is shorter than the travel time needed to fill the whole source? Can cold-front-driven gas sloshing in the intracluster medium supply enough turbulence to re-accelerate seed electrons from the central active galactic nucleus across the observed mini-halo volume?

evidence.quote: In very few relaxed clusters, the central radio AGN is surrounded by di ﬀuse emission in the form of a halo, with steep spectral index ( α > 1), and linear extent of the order of few hundreds of kpc.

Only 9 mini–halos are known to date ( Giacintucci et al. 2011b and references therein), and their origin is an issue, since the di ﬀusion time of the relativistic electrons is shorter than the travel time necessary to cover the whole extent of these sources.

Cold fronts in the ICM have been observed in some clusters hosting a mini–halo, suggesting that gas sloshing may be responsible for the origin of the cold fronts and may provide the turbulence needed to re–accelerate seed electrons, most likely coming from the radio activity of the central AGN, to form a mini–halo

accepted.question_text: Do galaxy clusters that host ultra-steep-spectrum radio halos, meaning radio halos with GHz-frequency synchrotron spectral index around α ∼ 2 under the convention S ∝ ν^-α, have basic differences from galaxy clusters that host “classical” radio halos with typical spectral-index values around 1.2–1.4?

evidence.quote: It is presently unclear if there are basic diﬀerences between clusters with ultra steep spectrum radio halos and those hosting “classical” ones, and it is unknown if less energetic mergers result in an observational signature in the radio band.
It has also become clear that a large distribution exists for the spectral index of the synchrotron spectrum of radio halos, and sources with α up to ∼2 (S∝ν−α) have been recently found.

Beyond the historical sources, most of the radio halos known so far were found either by inspection of relatively shallow surveys, such as the 1.4 GHz Northern VLA Sky Survey (NVSS) and the 327 MHz Westerbork Northern Sky Survey (WENSS) ( Giovannini et al. 1999 and Kempner & Sarazin 2001 respectively), leading to the detection of relatively bright sources at GHz frequencies, which do have spectral index values in the range 1.2–1.4, as often reported in the literature.

accepted.question_text: Do less energetic cluster mergers, including common minor mergers expected to dominate mass assembly in the Universe, produce observable signatures in the radio band? If they do, are those signatures manifested as ultra-steep-spectrum radio halos or other faint diffuse cluster radio sources that are preferentially detectable with high-sensitivity low-frequency observations and constrained at GHz frequencies?
accepted.context_brief: Radio signatures of less energetic mergers

evidence.quote: It is presently unclear if there are basic diﬀerences between clusters with ultra steep spectrum radio halos and those hosting “classical” ones, and it is unknown if less energetic mergers result in an observational signature in the radio band.

An application of the turbulent re–acceleration model (Cassano 2010b) shows that a population of ultra–steep spectrum radio halos is expected, as due to to less energetic mergers and /or less massive clusters.

According to the statistical results of Cassano et al. (2010b), such objects should open up the study of the observational eﬀects of the common and numerous minor mergers, expected to be the dominant mechanisms of mass assembly in the Universe.
The fewµJy sensitivity of the EVLA will lead to the detection of very faint halos at GHz frequencies, thus constraining the bright end of the radio spectrum of ultra–steep sources.

accepted.question_text: For radio halos and relics in galaxy clusters, what are their well-defined integrated radio spectra from roughly hundred-MHz frequencies to GHz frequencies, and what do the spectral shapes and spectral-index values reveal about the underlying relativistic electron population and the re-acceleration processes that generate the diffuse emission?
accepted.context_brief: Integrated spectra of halos and relics

evidence.quote: Well deﬁned radio spectra, from ∼hundred MHz to GHz frequencies and good spectral imaging are available o nly for few halos and relics, and such information is crucial for a detailed understandin g of their origin.
The accurate measurement of the integrated spectra of radio halos is a di ﬃcult task.

It is essential to increase the number of radio halos and relics with well deﬁned integrated spectra, since the spectral shape and spectral index value are the signature of the underlying electron population and of the re–acceleration processes.

accepted.question_text: What is the spatial distribution of radio spectral index within diffuse cluster radio sources, and how can spectral-index imaging be used to understand both the integrated spectral behavior of radio halos and relics and the distribution of magnetic fields throughout the cluster volume?

evidence.quote: Imaging of the spectral index distribution provides information on the energy spectrum of the radiating electrons and on the magnetic ﬁeld distribution.

Imaging of the spectral index distribution is another crucial piece of information which we still miss. It is relevant not only to address point (2), but also for the study the distribution of the magnetic ﬁeld in the cluster volume.

accepted.question_text: Which galaxy clusters contain both a firmly detected shock front and a radio relic with a clear spatial and physical connection, and does a larger sample of such systems support the view that relics are produced by merger-driven shocks with Mach numbers less than or approximately equal to 3?

evidence.quote: The location, shape and polarization properties of relics suggest that their origin is connected to the propagation of shock waves, with Mach numbers <∼3, during cluster mergers.

For a few well studied cases, the spectrum of the radio halo is consistent with Mach numbers for the shock in the range 1–3 (i.e. A 521, Giacintucci et al. 2008; CIZA J2242.8+5301, van Weeren et al. 2010; A 754, Macario et al. 2011).

So far only a few shocks have been ﬁrmly detected with Chandra (Markevitch et al., present volume), and it would be crucial to increase the statistics not only of conﬁrmed shocks, but also of clusters with a clear connection between a shock front and a relic, as it has been the case for A 520 (Markevitch et al. 2005) and A 754 (Macario et al. 2011).

accepted.question_text: What do galaxy clusters that contain multiple diffuse radio sources reveal about how shocks and turbulence develop throughout the cluster volume during cluster mergers, and how do those merger-driven processes imprint themselves on the observed diffuse radio emission?
accepted.context_brief: Multiple diffuse sources in merging clusters

evidence.quote: The number of clusters with multiple diffuse sources is steadily increasing, especially after the advent of the good quality images provided by the GMRT at low frequencies (see for instance van Weeren at al., present volume).
This is most likely telling us something about the development of shocks and turbulence in the cluster volume as consequence of cluster mergers, and their signature on the di ﬀuse radio emission.

accepted.question_text: Are ultra-steep-spectrum radio halos a genuine population of diffuse cluster radio sources rather than only two confirmed objects, and would finding more such halos provide observational support for the turbulent re-acceleration model of radio-halo formation?
accepted.context_brief: Population status of ultra-steep-spectrum radio halos

evidence.quote: So far only two radio halos are conﬁrmed ultra–steep spectrum sources. It is essential that more objects are found, to safely talk of a “new population”.
Finding more USSRH would provide further observational support in favour of the turbulent re–acceleration model.
LOFAR has started to deliver the ﬁrst images (see Rottgering, present volume), and it is expected to unveil the population of ultra–steep spectrum halos which the GMRT has just discovered.

trace.notes: Resolved arXiv abs URL to the PDF, downloaded it locally, and mapped the 8-page PDF. Likely open-question regions were the abstract, Section 2.2 on mini-halos, Section 4 on spectra, Section 5 on relics and shocks, and Section 6 on open questions and future perspectives.
Extracted explicit unresolved issues about ultra-steep-spectrum versus classical radio-halo host clusters, less energetic mergers, and missing radio spectra or spectral imaging.
Extracted the mini-halo origin problem because the source explicitly states that their origin is an issue and gives the electron-diffusion-time difficulty.
Extracted missing integrated spectra and spectral-index imaging as candidate observational questions because the source emphasizes that such measurements are available for only a handful of halos.
Extracted the shock-front/radio-relic connection as an open observational question because the source says only a few shocks have been firmly detected and more shock-relic associations are needed.

Extracted the four numbered future-perspective points: low-frequency imaging and the ultra-steep-spectrum population, integrated spectra, spectral-index maps, and multiple diffuse sources in merging clusters.

Expanded the mini-halo origin issue into a self-contained question by inlining the relaxed-cluster setting, central radio AGN, steep spectrum, size scale, diffusion-time obstacle, and proposed gas-sloshing/turbulent re-acceleration mechanism from the cited evidence.

Rewrote the source's direct statement about unclear differences between ultra-steep-spectrum and classical radio-halo host clusters, adding only spectral-index definitions supported by the abstract and Section 4.1.
Combined the abstract's less-energetic-merger question with Section 4.1 and Section 6 evidence connecting ultra-steep-spectrum halos to less energetic or minor mergers and faint radio signatures.

Rewrote the missing integrated-spectra issue as a question about measuring spectra from hundred-MHz to GHz frequencies and interpreting spectral shape and index in terms of electron populations and re-acceleration.
Expanded the missing spectral-index imaging issue using the source's stated links to radiating electron spectra and magnetic-field distribution.
Rewrote the relics-and-shocks section into a self-contained question about building a larger sample of firm shock-front/radio-relic connections and testing merger-shock interpretations.
Rewrote the multiple-diffuse-source point as a question about what such clusters reveal about shock and turbulence development and their radio signatures.

Separated the population-status question for ultra-steep-spectrum radio halos from the host-cluster-difference question because Section 6 treats discovery of more USSRH as its own observational test of the turbulent re-acceleration model.

Merged overlapping spectrum-measurement candidates into q_004 and kept the host-cluster comparison, minor-merger signature, and population-status questions separate because they ask for distinct outcomes.

Accepted eight questions. Each accepted item is self-contained, contains no source-pointing language in question_text, includes verbatim page-numbered evidence, introduces no unsupported technical facts, and has solved-status metadata set to false because the source does not explicitly mark any item solved.
